question: What are the time and space complexity of using a comparison sort like `arr.sort()` on an array of n elements?
options: O(N) time, O(1) space, always
Typically O(N log N) time for comparison-based sorts like merge sort/quicksort (average case), with O(N) or O(log N) additional space depending on the algorithm
O(N^2) time in every case, regardless of algorithm
O(1) time regardless of array size
explanation: Efficient comparison-based sorting algorithms (merge sort, quicksort, heapsort) achieve O(N log N) average-case time. Space varies: merge sort typically needs O(N) auxiliary space, while quicksort's recursion stack is roughly O(log N) on average.

question: Why can a naive recursive Fibonacci implementation like `fib(n) = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2)` become extremely slow and memory-intensive for even moderately large n?
options: It's actually O(n) time and very efficient
It recomputes the same subproblems exponentially many times (O(2^n) time), and can build up a deep call stack, consuming significant time and stack space
JavaScript doesn't support recursion at all
It only fails for negative inputs
explanation: This naive version recalculates fib(n-2) many times across different branches of recursion, leading to roughly O(2^n) redundant calls. Memoizing previously computed results (or using an iterative approach) brings this down to O(n) time.

question: What is the average time complexity of a get/set (lookup/insert) operation on a hash map?
options: O(n), since it must always scan every entry
O(1) on average, since a well-distributed hash function maps keys directly to a bucket location without needing to search the whole structure
O(log n), the same as a balanced binary search tree
O(n^2) in all cases
explanation: Hash maps compute a key's bucket location directly via a hash function, giving average O(1) lookup/insert — though worst-case (with many hash collisions) can degrade to O(n) for a poorly designed hash function or adversarial input.

question: What is a strict prerequisite for binary search to work correctly, and what time complexity does it achieve?
options: No prerequisite is needed; it works on any array in O(1) time
The array must already be sorted; it achieves O(log n) time by repeatedly halving the search range
The array must contain only unique values, and it runs in O(n) time
It requires a linked list, not an array
explanation: Binary search relies on being able to eliminate half the remaining elements at each step based on an ordering comparison — which is only valid if the data is already sorted. This halving gives it O(log n) time complexity, dramatically faster than a linear O(n) scan for large datasets.

question: How does memoization improve a naive exponential-time recursive algorithm like Fibonacci?
options: It has no effect on time complexity, only readability
It caches the results of subproblems already solved, so each unique subproblem is computed only once — reducing Fibonacci from O(2^n) down to O(n) time (at the cost of O(n) extra space for the cache)
It removes the need for recursion entirely
It only works for sorting algorithms
explanation: By storing each computed fib(n) result the first time it's calculated, memoization ensures the function never redoes the same work twice — turning an exponential blow-up of repeated subproblems into a linear number of unique computations, trading some extra memory for a massive time improvement.

question: Why is `array.push()` in JavaScript typically described as O(1) 'amortized', even though the underlying array occasionally needs to be resized and copied?
options: Resizing never actually happens in JavaScript arrays
Most push() calls are truly O(1), and the occasional expensive O(n) resize-and-copy operation is 'spread out' (amortized) across many pushes, averaging out to O(1) per operation over a long sequence
push() is actually O(n) every single time
Amortized means the operation is always instant regardless of size
explanation: When an array's backing storage is full, adding one more element requires allocating a bigger block and copying everything over — an O(n) operation. But this happens rarely (e.g. only when capacity doubles), so averaged ('amortized') across a long sequence of pushes, the cost per push works out to O(1).

question: What is a classic example of a deliberate space-time tradeoff in algorithm design?
options: Always minimizing both time and space simultaneously with no compromise possible
Precomputing and caching results in a lookup table (using more memory) so future queries can be answered instantly instead of recalculating from scratch each time
Using recursion instead of loops
Reducing the number of variables in a function
explanation: Caching/memoization is a textbook space-time tradeoff: you spend extra memory storing previously computed results in order to save significant computation time on repeated or related future requests — a very common and deliberate engineering choice.

question: What is the time complexity of two nested loops, each independently iterating n times, where the inner loop body does constant-time work?
options: O(n)
O(n^2), since the inner loop's n iterations happen for each of the outer loop's n iterations
O(log n)
O(2n)
explanation: The inner loop runs n times for every single iteration of the outer loop (which itself runs n times), giving n × n = n² total iterations of constant work — O(n²) overall.

question: Quicksort has an average time complexity of O(n log n), but its worst case is O(n²). When does this worst case typically occur?
options: Quicksort never has a worst case; it's always O(n log n)
When the chosen pivot consistently produces very unbalanced partitions (e.g. picking the first element as pivot on an already-sorted array), causing the recursion depth to approach n instead of log n
Only when the array contains negative numbers
Only on arrays smaller than 10 elements
explanation: Quicksort's efficiency depends on the pivot roughly splitting the array in half each time. If the pivot selection strategy consistently picks a poor pivot (e.g. always the smallest or largest remaining element, which can happen on already-sorted input with a naive 'first element' pivot choice), partitions become highly unbalanced and the algorithm degrades to O(n²).

question: Why does Big-O notation ignore constant factors and lower-order terms (e.g. treating `3n² + 5n + 100` simply as `O(n²)`)?
options: It's a mistake in how Big-O is commonly taught

Big-O describes how an algorithm's cost scales as input size grows very large, and at that scale the highest-order term dominates growth, making constants and smaller terms comparatively insignificant
Constants and lower-order terms are actually the most important part of performance analysis
It only applies to algorithms written in compiled languages
explanation: Big-O is about asymptotic growth — how running time or space scales as input size (n) approaches infinity. At large n, an n² term overwhelmingly dominates a 5n term or a constant 100, so those details are dropped to focus on the term that determines how the algorithm scales.

question: What's the time complexity tradeoff between inserting an element at the front of a linked list versus at the front of a plain array?
options: Both are O(1) with no meaningful difference
Inserting at the front of a linked list is O(1) (just repoint a pointer), while inserting at the front of an array is O(n), since every existing element must shift over by one position
Both operations are O(n) in every language
Linked lists cannot support front insertion at all
explanation: A linked list's head insertion just creates a new node pointing to the old head — O(1). An array, being contiguous memory, must shift every existing element one slot to the right to make room at index 0, which is O(n) in the worst case.

question: Merge sort splits an array in half recursively (log n levels of splitting) and does O(n) work merging at each level. Why does this result in O(n log n) overall, rather than O(n) or O(log n)?
code:
// log n levels of recursion, each doing O(n) total merge work across that level
function mergeSort(arr) { /* ... */ }
options: Because you multiply the O(n) work done at each level by the log n number of levels, giving O(n log n) total
Because n and log n are added together, not multiplied
Merge sort is actually O(n), not O(n log n)
The number of levels is always n, not log n
explanation: Each level of the recursion tree (there are log n levels, since the array halves each time) requires O(n) total work to merge all the pieces at that level back together. Multiplying the per-level cost (n) by the number of levels (log n) gives the overall O(n log n) complexity.

question: What is the time complexity of a standard breadth-first search (BFS) or depth-first search (DFS) traversal on a graph with V vertices and E edges?
options: O(V) only, ignoring edges entirely
O(V + E), since the algorithm visits every vertex once and examines every edge once while exploring
O(V × E), since every vertex must check every edge individually
O(log V), similar to binary search
explanation: Both BFS and DFS visit each vertex exactly once and traverse each edge exactly once (to discover neighboring vertices), giving a combined complexity of O(V + E) — linear in the total size of the graph's vertices and edges.

question: If you need to repeatedly check whether a value exists in a growing collection, why would using a Set (or object/dictionary) instead of an array's `.includes()` meaningfully improve performance?
options: There's no performance difference between the two approaches
Array.includes() must scan up to every element (O(n) per check), while a Set's hash-based lookup is O(1) on average, which matters a lot when doing many repeated lookups
Set can only store numbers, not strings or objects
Array.includes() is always faster because arrays are contiguous in memory
explanation: Array.includes() performs a linear scan in the worst case — O(n) per call. A Set uses a hash table internally, giving average O(1) membership checks. For code that performs many repeated 'does this exist?' checks, switching from an array to a Set can turn an O(n²) pattern into O(n).

question: Which underlying data structure is typically used to implement breadth-first search (BFS), and which is used for depth-first search (DFS)?
options: BFS uses a stack; DFS uses a queue
BFS uses a queue (explore level by level, first-in-first-out); DFS uses a stack, or equivalently the function call stack via recursion (explore as deep as possible before backtracking)
Both use exactly the same data structure with no difference
Neither requires any auxiliary data structure
explanation: BFS explores all neighbors at the current depth before going deeper, which naturally matches a queue's first-in-first-out order. DFS dives as deep as possible down one path before backtracking, which matches a stack's last-in-first-out order — often implemented implicitly via recursive function calls.
